reference.source: Valvular and congenital heart disease references
clinicalPearls: Backflow across the pulmonary valve, very often iatrogenic after repair of tetralogy of Fallot or pulmonary valvotomy
Other causes include pulmonary hypertension, endocarditis and congenital valve abnormalities
Mild pulmonary regurgitation is common and usually of no consequence
Chronic severe regurgitation causes progressive right ventricular dilatation and eventual dysfunction
The murmur is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge (a Graham Steell murmur when due to pulmonary hypertension)
Timing of pulmonary valve replacement in post-tetralogy patients is guided by right ventricular size and function on cardiac MRI
reference.pathophysiology: Pulmonary regurgitation occurs when the pulmonary valve fails to prevent diastolic backflow from the pulmonary artery into the right ventricle. The commonest setting is after surgical relief of right ventricular outflow obstruction (as in tetralogy of Fallot), where the valve is rendered incompetent. The regurgitant volume chronically overloads the right ventricle, causing progressive dilatation; over years this leads to right ventricular dysfunction, exercise intolerance and an increased risk of arrhythmia. Pulmonary hypertension can also cause functional regurgitation through pulmonary artery and annular dilatation.
additionalDifferentials: Residual lesions after congenital heart surgery
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography assessing the valve and right ventricle
Cardiac MRI to quantify regurgitant fraction and right ventricular volumes
redFlags: Progressive right ventricular dilatation or dysfunction
Exercise intolerance or arrhythmia in post-tetralogy patients
reference.prognosis: Mild pulmonary regurgitation is benign, but chronic severe regurgitation after congenital repair can cause right ventricular decline; timely pulmonary valve replacement can preserve or improve right ventricular function.
pitfalls: Dismissing chronic severe regurgitation because symptoms appear late
Relying on echocardiography alone without MRI for right ventricular assessment
Delaying valve replacement until right ventricular dysfunction is irreversible
Confusing the murmur with aortic regurgitation
management: Manage mild regurgitation with reassurance and periodic surveillance, as it is usually benign and needs no intervention
Undertake pulmonary valve replacement, surgical or percutaneous, in chronic severe regurgitation guided by right ventricular size and function, particularly after tetralogy of Fallot repair
Relieve right heart failure symptoms with diuretic therapy
Treat any underlying cause, including pulmonary hypertension driving functional regurgitation and infective endocarditis
Monitor for and manage atrial and ventricular arrhythmias with rhythm monitoring and antiarrhythmic or ablation therapy
Follow up with serial cardiac MRI to quantify the regurgitant fraction and right ventricular volumes and time intervention
Manage within a specialist adult congenital heart disease service
